title: C4828 — Active Noise Control Microphone Left Rear
introduction:
I use this reference as a seating chart for the left-rear active noise control microphone’s connections: the drawing locates each cavity, and the matching table row explains its electrical role. Start with the connector identity table, match a cavity label to its row, then read across to the circuit, wire description, function and terminal information. The positive and negative microphone labels belong together; they are not instructions to connect either wire to chassis ground.

This page supports identification and circuit-map reading. Access, connector release, physical viewing direction, electrical testing and replacement are outside its scope. Gauge conventions and the Box and Size codes are not defined here, so leave those entries uninterpreted rather than using them to choose wire or tools.

edits.why: I use the housing outline to keep my place in the drawing, then match its cavity labels to the table below. As drawn, the cavities form a vertical column, with the shaded position at the bottom. That shading corresponds to the row without an assigned circuit. This describes the illustration’s layout; it does not establish how to hold or approach the installed connector.

edits.text: Read the cavity and circuit map
edits.why: Cavity links the drawing to the table; Circuit Number identifies the electrical path. Read Color, Gauge, Function and Terminal Part Number across that same row so details from neighboring circuits do not get mixed together. The populated rows distinguish the positive and negative microphone connections, while the blank circuit row and its Used entry identify the unused position. These assignments describe connections, not whether the microphone is working.

A pigtail is the connector with attached wire leads. I cross-check the overview’s Kit List and Hard Shell fields against the service table’s Number and Engineering Shell fields; Service Part identifies the listed service assembly. The Image field names an asset rather than adding another instruction. The pigtail and circuit Gauge entries belong to separate records, so their difference alone supplies no wire-substitution or splice rule.
